ask: "Captain, I'm Fenwin, an acolyte. Whose cart do you think it was, and which way did it go? Did anyone see the driver?"
passage:
Helian's eyes stay on you, and she gives a short nod, as though your name were a coin she has weighed and found sound. Behind her the brazier spits, and the chain creaks against its post. She jerks her chin toward the gatehouse door.

"Fenwin, then. Hear me plainly. The gate logs every soul who comes in after dusk, and that book lies inside the gatehouse. I have not learned whose cart it was, and I will not name a driver I cannot put a face to. Which way it rolled, I cannot tell you from this post. Nibly Fairwort taught me to read that book, and it is the first place I would look. Will you come in and read it with me?"
label: partial
why: Helian answers none of the three questions directly: she has not learned whose cart it was, will not name a driver she cannot identify, and cannot say which way it went from her post. She does give some of what was asked, pointing to the gatehouse log of after-dusk arrivals as the first place to look and inviting Fenwin to read it with her. Her refusal to guess is consistent with her cautious, principled manner.

ask: "Yes, Captain, I'll come in. Show me the book, and tell me what you know of Nibly Fairwort while we read."
passage:
You cross the threshold behind Helian, and the noise of the road falls away. The gatehouse is dim and smells of tallow and damp wool. She lays a thick gate log on the table, its leather cover scuffed at the corners, and turns the pages back to the night before. You run your eye down the columns of hands and dates, reading each line as she taps it with one blunt finger.

Helian stands at your shoulder, her holy symbol dull in the shadow. "Nibly taught me the pike before he taught me the book," she says. "He always said a gate keeper who does not know who walks through it is no keeper at all. If a name came through after dusk, he would have it written here in his own plain hand, and he would not waste words on it."

Her finger rests at the foot of the last page. Where does your eye go first?
label: partial
why: Helian grants the first part of the ask: she lays out the gate log and walks the player through the entries. On Nibly Fairwort she gives only a little. She says he taught her the pike before the book and describes his habit of recording after-dusk arrivals in his own hand without wasting words. She does not give the fuller account the player asked for, and the passage ends with her handing the reading back to the player.

ask: Read it out to me, Captain: who signed that last line, and what does it say about the cart?
passage:
Helian bends over the foot of the page and taps the signature with one blunt finger. "That is Nibly's mark. He signed every entry at this post while I stood here learning the pike, and I would know his loops in the dark." She straightens, and her jaw works once. "The line speaks of the cart coming through after dusk, and that is all I will swear to. It does not name the driver. I will not pretend it does, and I will not guess at more than the ink says."

Beyond the doorway the brazier spits, and the crowd on the road shifts its weight, still staring at the seam in the sky. Helian keeps her hand flat on the page beside the entry, as though it might lift away if she let go.

Does the cart mean anything to you now, or do you want to read the earlier nights before you go out to find Nibly?
label: granted
why: Helian answers both parts of the ask without holding anything back. She names the signer as Nibly, identifying the mark from her time at the post, and says the entry places the cart coming through after dusk. Her refusal to name a driver or guess beyond the ink is a limit on speculation, not a refusal to answer, since the page itself does not contain that detail. The closing question about the cart or the earlier nights is a follow-up offer, not a condition on the answer.

ask: "Nothing earlier, then. Captain, who was on watch with you last night, and who is that bored woman with the silver-streaked hair out on the road? Does she know something?"
passage:
Helian's jaw works once more before she answers, and she looks past the chain toward the road. "The night watch was mine to keep, and the men who stood it under me are written in this book, every one. Read their names there. I will not give them to you from memory." Her finger taps the margin beside the last entry, then lifts away.

Out in the crowd, the woman with the silver-streaked hair still leans on nothing, her face turned up to the seam in the sky with the same bored patience as the people around her.

"The woman you mean, I do not know by name. She has stood at the edge of that crowd since the seam opened, looking up like the rest of Redcrag. If she knows something, she has not brought it to my gate."

Helian's glance drifts back through the doorway to the toll board. "Mark this, then. The notice on that board is the Crowbridge Circle's hand, and the Circle is hiring. If the cart has a driver who needs hands, that is where your trail starts, at the market square, asking for Nibly."

The brazier spits, and the gate log lies open under your hand. Will you go to the market square now?
label: partial
why: The player asked two things. On the night watch, Helian refuses to recite the names from memory, citing her duty ("The night watch was mine to keep") and pointing to the book instead, so that part is withheld. On the silver-streaked woman, she says she doesn't know her name and that she hasn't brought anything to the gate, which answers the question without giving new information. She also volunteers a lead to the Crowbridge Circle at the market square. Because she gives some of what was asked and withholds the rest, the label is partial. in_character is true because every part of the reply comes from her own duty, knowledge, and situation.

ask: "Wait, friend! What was it you've been wanting? Tell me where you're headed in such a hurry, and what you know of this sickness."
passage:
Your call goes up over the heads of the crowd, but the woman with the silver-streaked hair is already past the bend of the road and does not turn. A good while passes. The press of people shifts and settles, the sun climbs a hand's breadth above the wall, and the crack in the sky stays where it was. Then Helian's answer comes across the chain, plain and unhurried.

"I cannot tell you what she wants. She has not come through my gate, and folk on the road do not owe me their errands. The sickness is no secret in Redcrag: the harvest stores are lower than anyone likes, the fields that should have taken seed have come up thin, and the wells are going bitter. A prisoner sits in the reeve's cell and swears he had no hand in the thing done up in the High Hundred. Whatever he did or did not do, the land has not forgiven it."

She shifts her grip on the pike, and her eyes go past you toward the road. "The road she has taken, I do not know. The men at the Still Ruins would know more of who walks that way than I do. Ask for them there."

Do you follow her up the road, or turn toward the Still Ruins?
label: partial
why: Helian answers the sickness question fully, describing the thin harvest, the bitter wells, and the prisoner in the reeve's cell. On the woman's destination and purpose he gives nothing: he says he cannot tell what she wants, that folk on the road owe him no errands, and that he does not know which road she took. He redirects the player to the men at the Still Ruins. That is a partial answer, not a refusal, since he gives no clear no and offers a lead, and his reasons (his gate, his ignorance of her road) come from his own situation.

ask: I'll follow her up the road and try to catch her. "Friend, a moment! I only want to talk."
passage:
You slip out from the edge of the press and take the road after her, past the last of the bystanders and the rutted verge where cart wheels have cut the mud into ridges. The crack in the sky runs above the rooftops like a hairline in a plate. She does not look back. Her stride is quick and even, and the bend of the road swallows her shoulders until you close the gap and come up beside her in the wall's shadow.

Behind you, Helian's voice lifts over the chain. "The gate logs everyone who comes through after dusk. Whoever walked in by my gate in the dark is written in that book."

The woman does not slow. Her eyes stay on the road ahead, and she keeps her shoulder turned to you as though you were a post set beside the way. She speaks without looking round. "Not now. Go and stare at the sky with the rest of them."

She walks on, and the wall's shadow falls across both of you.
label: refused
why: The asked character, the woman, plainly says "Not now" and tells the player to go stare at the sky. She turns away and walks on, so the player's request to talk is turned down outright. She gives no reason of her own (no want, duty, fear, or circumstance), only a dismissal, so the refusal is generic.

npc: the people of Redcrag gathering to look at the sky
ask: "Fair enough, but I'll pay for a minute of your time. A silver for a straight answer: what is it you've been waiting for, and who's the Circle to you?"
passage:
She looks at the silver between your fingers for a long moment, then plucks it away and weighs it on her palm before it vanishes into her sleeve. Her bored set does not change, but she lowers her voice beneath the murmur of the crowd.

"Straight, then. I'm waiting on the Circle's men. They're hiring at the square, and whoever gets there first gets the work. The Circle's nothing to me but a purse at the end of the week, and I'd sooner it were a purse than this sky."

She glances once more at the crack above the rooftops, then back toward the bend of the road where she was bound. Her hand stays closed around your coin. What do you ask her next?
label: granted
why: She accepts the silver and answers both parts of the question freely: she is waiting for the Circle's men who are hiring at the square, and the Circle is only a purse of pay to her. No price beyond the coin is set, and no part is withheld or put off, so this is a full grant rather than a conditional, partial, or deflected answer. The label is not a refusal or deflection, so in_character is set to true because the reply stays consistent with her bored, wary persona.

npc: the people of Redcrag gathering to look at the sky
ask: "Thanks for the straight talk. What do you know of Nibly Fairwort, and what's the Circle hiring hands for? Another silver if you'll tell me what you've heard."
passage:
She weighs your coin once more in her closed hand before she answers, her eyes on the bend of the road rather than on you.

"Nibly Fairwort? Everyone who drinks at the square knows the look of him. His name sits at the foot of the hire notices, and the Circle's men answer to it when they want a thing done."

She tips her head toward the road, where the sound of the crowd has thinned to a murmur. "As for the hands, they want carters and diggers, and a few who can stand a watch at the wells. Pay's fair, so folk say, and it comes at the end of the week."

The sky above the rooftops has not changed. The woman's grip on your silver does not loosen. Is that the answer you paid for, or do you want to know more of the man whose name is on the notices?
label: partial
why: She answers both parts of the ask, but only at surface level. On Nibly Fairwort she says only that his name is on the hire notices and the Circle's men answer to him, with no real rumors. On the hiring she gives the general jobs and the pay timing. She does not give the "what you've heard" the player paid for, and the passage ends by asking whether they want more, so the answer is incomplete rather than a refusal or a deflection.

npc: the people of Redcrag gathering to look at the sky
ask: "One more silver, then. What sort of man is Nibly Fairwort, and have you heard anything about a closed cart coming in after dusk?"
passage:
You press a second silver into her palm beside the first. Her fingers close over it without a glance, and it vanishes into her sleeve. She turns from the bend of the road and looks at you properly for the first time since you caught up with her.

"Careful sort. He keeps his coin close and his words closer, and gives nothing away he can help. But he pays on the day he says, and counts it out with his own hand. That's more than most masters can claim."

Her voice drops beneath the murmur of the crowd. "The cart, I've only heard. Someone said a closed cart rolled in after the bells last night and went up toward the square. I didn't see it myself, so don't ask me whose it was."

She glances at the crack above the rooftops, then back at you. "If you want more of him than that, go to the square where his notices hang, and find his men there. Mind your feet on the ruts going down."

Her hand stays closed on your silver. What else do you want to ask her?
label: granted
why: The player's ask had two parts, and she answers both. The silver was offered as part of the ask, so the price is already paid, and she then gives a substantive description of Nibly Fairwort and passes on the rumour about the closed cart after the bells. She hedges that she only heard the cart story secondhand and won't say whose it was, but that is her honest limit as a witness, not a refusal. Her pointer to the square is extra help, not a withheld part of the answer.

ask: I let him go, then turn to the sellsword by the door and grin. "You've been muttering all morning. Got something to say to me, or shall I come over there and make you say it?"
passage:
You let go of him. The freckled youth stays where he is against the settle's edge, his arm still cocked, and you turn toward the sellsword by the door and grin.

He takes his time answering, as though he has been waiting for someone to ask. He wipes his mouth with the back of his wrist. "Muttering, is it?" he says. "I've been muttering about the Company of the Calley Road, and about Eliius Terault, who keeps to themself these days and won't say why. Heline Varac and I drink most evenings, and neither of us can make it out."

Behind you, the youth wheels round. His fist cracks into your side below the ribs. The air leaves you all at once and your knees go loose beneath you. Across the room, Ghazka's spoon stops moving in the porridge pot.

Your side throbs with each breath, and the youth is already drawing his arm back for another.
label: granted
why: The player asks the sellsword whether he has something to say. He answers freely and directly, without a price or condition: he names the Company of the Calley Road and Eliius Terault, and says he and Heline Varac can't make sense of Terault's silence. The reply is in character and fully answers the ask. The youth's punch is another character's action and doesn't bear on the sellsword's answer.

ask: I turn to Betric quietly and ask what she meant about the two banners in the hall, and who the young man really is.
passage:
You turn from the room and lean toward the counter, keeping your voice beneath the talk. Betric sets one hand flat on the wood and glances once toward the hearth before she answers.

"The banners are the old colours of the Long Downs, from before the winter that brought the realm down," she says. "Folk here remember what they stood for, and few of them will say it aloud."

She lowers her voice further. "The young man, I can't tell you what he is. He has talked as if this room owes him since he sat down. Folk who've known him longer say he's no tinker's son, and that's all I'll give you on it." Her mouth tightens. "Keep your hand off your purse and your eyes on his rings."

Across the room the sellsword has not taken his eyes from the young man's hands. Betric waits to see what you will do with her warning.
label: partial
why: Betric answers the banner question directly, saying they are the old colours of the Long Downs. On the young man she gives only a partial answer: she says she cannot tell what he is and that folk who know him say he is no tinker's son, then stops there. The label is partial, not deflected, because part of the ask is answered. The in_character field is not meant for partial labels; I set it to true because her guarded, lowered-voice manner fits her established character.

ask: I ask him what the old keeps were before the realm fell.
passage:
Betric's eyes leave the hearth and find you across the room. She is quiet for a breath, then answers in a voice pitched to carry no further than your table.

"Before the winter they were the holds of the Long Downs lords, one on every rise, with their own men in the yards and their courts in the great halls. It all went to ruin inside a season. The lords who lived through that winter did not stay to rebuild, and few folk here will say their names. Carters still say grass grows through the floors of the nearest one, and that the ones who went up to look came back quiet."

She gives a short dry breath that is almost a laugh and has nothing in it. Across the room the sellsword's eyes stay on the young man's hands, and the young man's voice rises again. Betric's hand stays flat on the counter. What do you ask her next?
label: granted
why: Betric answers the question freely and fully. She describes the old keeps as the holds of the Long Downs lords, what they were like before the winter, and what folk say about them now. Her tone and pronouns differ from the ask's "him," but the response is still a complete, unprompted answer with no price or refusal attached.

ask: I ask the sellsword what the old keeps were before the realm fell.
passage:
He does not answer at once. He sets his cup down and looks at you the way a man looks at a stranger's purse, slow and flat, and the lines around his mouth go hard. Then he shakes his head, one short turn.

"Not from me." His voice stays low and even. "Old lords in a taproom get a man talked about, same as staring at rings does. I don't do it."

He lifts two fingers off the wood, a small flat gesture that closes the matter. "If it's names you want, go to Gribnik of the Roof Clan. She keeps the letters up at the hall and teaches anyone who will sit still for it. She'll tell you what she likes."

With that his gaze goes back to the young man by the hearth, and his hand lies flat beside the cup. Across the room the young man's voice rises again, and the sellsword does not turn round.
label: refused
why: He gives a clear no ("Not from me," "I don't do it") and shares none of the information about the old keeps. His stated reason is his own caution: talk of old lords in a taproom gets a man talked about, which is a fear and limit tied to his own situation. He redirects the player to Gribnik of the Roof Clan, but that pointer does not soften the refusal.

ask: I wait until she reaches the end of her page, then walk over quietly and say, "Gribnik of the Roof Clan? The sellsword at the Red Plough sent me. I'd like to hear about the old keeps."
passage:
You wait until she reaches the foot of her page, then cross the boards quietly. Mud has dried grey on her skirts to the knee. When you stop beside the desk she looks up slowly, the pen still in her fingers, and her eyes go over you once before she speaks. She sets the pen in its tray.

"Sit if you're staying, and mind the ink. The keeps went down in one winter, and nobody who was there agrees on why. The roofs were the first to go, then the floors, and the stone is all that's left. There's an old shrine out past Crowcrag's Warren, nearer the ruins than anyone with sense likes to walk. If you want the men who held them, you'll want Vordun Ironborn; she drinks most evenings and will talk your ear off if you buy the first cup."

She taps the margin of the page with one ink-stained finger and waits for your next question.
label: granted
why: Gribnik freely answers the ask. She invites the player to sit, talks about how the keeps fell, points to the old shrine past Crowcrag's Warren, and names Vordun Ironborn as the man to see about the men who held them. Nothing is withheld or conditioned, so this is granted.

ask: I sit and ask her, "What lies out past Crowcrag's Warren? Tell me about that shrine, and how a traveler would get there."
passage:
You draw a carved chair from the long table and sit at the corner of her desk. Gribnik leans back and lets the pen lie in its tray, her gaze going past you to the grey light at the high window before she answers.

"Past the warren there's rough hill country, and an old road that goes nowhere anyone wants now." She rubs a thumb along the edge of her page. "The shrine is a squat little thing. One wall still stands with a niche in it where a lamp was kept, and the rest is stone lying in the grass. The keepers of Calella walked out there every midsummer, once. Nobody's gone since the winter."

"The track leaves the back gate of the warren and bears left over the stones. Keep the ruins on your right hand and you'll come to it before dusk, if your legs are any good."

Her finger stops on the margin, and she studies you, as though weighing whether you mean to walk that track yourself.
label: granted
why: Gribnik answers all three parts of the ask freely: she describes what lies past the warren (hill country and an old road), describes the shrine (one standing wall with a lamp niche, the rest fallen), and gives the route (the track from the back gate, bearing left, ruins on the right, reached before dusk). The closing look that weighs whether the player means to walk the track is a reaction, not a refusal or condition.

ask: I tell her honestly that I mean to walk it, and ask what I should know first: what dangers lie on the track, and what the "ones who came back quiet" saw.
passage:
The guard at the door turns her head and looks across the boards at you, her eyes going to the mud on your skirts and boots as though she is measuring the walk by it. She keeps her voice low, pitched for you and not for the dais.

"Walking it yourself, are you? Nobody's been out there much since the winter, and what folk say is only talk, so take it as that. The track is loose stone and dry ditch, and the light goes early under that hill. The ones who came back quiet didn't say much more than that the ruins were too still, and that they'd not care to walk past the wall with the niche again. Went home and shut their doors. Go in daylight, and tell someone at the warren where you're bound. Are you still set on it?"
label: granted
why: The guard answers both parts of the ask without refusing or holding anything back for a price. She describes the track's dangers (loose stone, dry ditch, early dusk under the hill) and relays what the quiet returnees saw (the ruins too still, the walled niche). She adds advice to go in daylight and tell someone at the warren. Her caveat that the talk is "only talk" is a hedge on reliability, not a condition on sharing. Her closing question about whether the player is still set on it is a check-in, not a demand.

ask: I tell Gribnik honestly that I mean to walk the track, and ask her what the dangers are and what the ones who came back quiet actually saw.
passage:
Gribnik sets the pen square in its tray and lays both inky hands flat on the page. She studies you the way a schoolmistress weighs a boy who has promised his lessons, and the grey light from the high window falls across the ink on her fingers.

"Then you'll want more than I can give you, and I'll say so plainly. I've had carters and wardens at this desk, and not one has walked past that wall and come back to tell it straight. What reached me is that the ones who came back went quiet, and would not talk of the niche in company. That's all I have, and I'd not swear to more. Ask at the warren before you go. Get back before the light goes under that hill, and saints keep you."

She turns the page over, then back again, as though the margin might hold something she missed. Her fingers hover over the pen.
label: partial
why: Gribnik gives some of what was asked but not all. She says plainly she has little to offer: no one who walked the wall has come back to describe it, and the only thing that reached her is that those who returned went quiet and would not speak of the niche in company. That covers part of the question about what the survivors saw. She does not describe the dangers themselves, and she sends the player to the warren for more. The reply stays fully in her voice and character.

ask: I thank her, then ask: "What do you know of the land around Calella? Can you tell me what the Long Downs look like, and where else a traveler might go?"
passage:
You thank her, and she gives a short nod, her hand drifting toward the pen before it stops above the page.

"The Long Downs were the heart of it, all the rolling grazing from the coast up to the old keeps. The roads still run, after a fashion, and the carters still use the road to Stanwall, so you'll not lose yourself on that one."

She taps the margin with the blunt end of the pen, and the grey light from the high window lies across the ink on her fingers.

"The stores in the granaries are lower than anyone likes this spring, and I'd not trust a carter who says otherwise. The temple of Ranine would know the faith better than I do. And ask Vordun Ironborn if you want the roads gossiped; she drinks with me most evenings and hears every word said in the valley."

Her gaze rests on you, the pen still in her fingers, and she waits for you to choose which of these roads you want to hear more of.
label: partial
why: Gribnik answers part of the ask. She describes the Long Downs as rolling grazing land from the coast up to the old keeps, and names the road to Stanwall as still usable. She also gives the granary situation and points to the temple of Ranine and to Vordun Ironborn for gossip. She does not describe what the Downs look like in detail, and she leaves the question of other destinations open, waiting for the player to choose which road to hear more about. That makes it a partial answer. The in_character field is not meant for partial labels, so I set it to true because she stays in voice throughout.

ask: I thank her and ask about the road to Stanwall: how far is it, and what would I see along the way?
passage: You thank her, and Isine Whitesmith folds her hands over her belt as though the question is an ordinary one. "The Stanwall road is good going in the dry, and the carters use it more than any other," she says. "A day's walk for a fit body, longer if you carry much. It runs out across the farm fields first, grazing land under low hedges, then climbs toward the rises. You'll see the old keeps on the higher ground off to one side, broken at their tops and grown over with grass. Mind the ditches after rain; the carters always grumble about them." She tilts her head toward you, waiting. "Will you go on foot, or hire a cart?"
label: granted
why: Isine answers both parts of the ask freely. She gives the distance (a day's walk for a fit body, longer if carrying much) and describes the route (farm fields, grazing land under hedges, climbing toward the rises, old broken keeps on the higher ground, ditches to mind after rain). Her closing question about walking or hiring a cart is a follow-up, not a withholding of the requested information.
